q: In VED classification, a 'Vital' store item is one whose

options.A: cost is the highest among all items in stock
options.B: non-availability stops essential operations or production
options.C: consumption value is the lowest in the depot
options.D: purchase requires the longest administrative approval

q: ABC analysis classifies stores items on the basis of their

options.A: physical size and weight in the depot
options.B: criticality to train operations
options.C: annual consumption (usage) value
options.D: frequency of purchase orders placed

q: The re-order level of a store item is equal to

options.A: likely consumption during lead time plus safety stock
options.B: maximum level minus the economic order quantity
options.C: average monthly consumption multiplied by twelve
options.D: safety stock minus the minimum stock level

q: Safety stock is maintained primarily to

options.A: reduce the unit price through bulk purchase
options.B: meet the annual budget targets of the depot
options.C: dispose of surplus and obsolete stores
options.D: guard against uncertainties in demand and lead time

q: In stores provisioning, 'lead time' means the

options.A: shelf life of a perishable store item
options.B: interval between placing an order and receiving the material
options.C: warranty period given by the supplier
options.D: time taken to inspect material after receipt

q: The maximum stock level is fixed mainly to

options.A: prevent overstocking and blockage of capital
options.B: ensure the depot never runs out of stock
options.C: increase the number of purchase orders
options.D: reduce the inspection time for receipts

q: The minimum stock level represents the

options.A: quantity ordered in every purchase order
options.B: average stock held during the financial year
options.C: lowest stock normally held to meet emergency needs
options.D: stock reserved only for imported items

q: Demand forecasting for stores provisioning is mainly based on

options.A: the budget sanctioned for the current year
options.B: the number of suppliers registered with the railway
options.C: prevailing market prices of raw materials
options.D: past consumption trends and known future requirements

q: Provisioning review is carried out primarily to

options.A: increase the variety of items stocked
options.B: ensure requirements are realistic and avoid over or under-provisioning
options.C: speed up payment of suppliers' bills
options.D: transfer all slow-moving items to other railways

q: Annual estimates of stores are prepared on the basis of

options.A: last year's budget allocation alone
options.B: the personal judgment of the depot in-charge
options.C: past consumption, anticipated changes and outstanding dues
options.D: the total number of staff in the depot

q: In ABC analysis, 'A' category items are characterised by

options.A: a small percentage of items accounting for a large share of consumption value
options.B: a large number of items with negligible total value
options.C: items that are never consumed during the year
options.D: items purchased only once in five years

q: The degree of control exercised over 'C' category items in ABC analysis is

options.A: the tightest, with weekly review of every item
options.B: identical to that for 'A' category items
options.C: based on daily physical verification
options.D: simple and loose, since their value impact is low

q: In VED classification, shortage of an 'Essential' item

options.A: has no effect on operations at all
options.B: causes dislocation or delay of work but not a complete stoppage
options.C: stops all train operations immediately
options.D: only affects the appearance of finished work

q: In VED classification, 'Desirable' items are those whose shortage

options.A: stops production in the workshop
options.B: cancels all scheduled train services
options.C: has no serious immediate effect on operations
options.D: requires emergency purchase every time

q: VED classification is most useful for deciding

options.A: priority in provisioning and the level of safety stock for each item
options.B: the colour code to be painted on storage bins
options.C: the mode of transport for delivering items
options.D: the financial year in which to buy items

q: The re-order level of an item increases when the

options.A: unit price of the item falls
options.B: number of suppliers increases
options.C: inspection time after receipt is reduced
options.D: lead time for replenishment lengthens

q: Safety stock is generally kept at nil or very low level for

options.A: vital imported spares
options.B: desirable, low-criticality items
options.C: items with highly variable demand
options.D: items with long and uncertain lead time

q: The quantity to be ordered at each replenishment is decided by considering the

options.A: seniority of the indenting officer
options.B: total plinth area of the depot
options.C: economic order quantity balancing ordering and carrying costs
options.D: number of holidays in the coming year

q: The economic order quantity is the order size at which

options.A: the total of ordering cost and carrying cost is minimum
options.B: the supplier offers the maximum discount
options.C: the depot godown is completely filled
options.D: only one order is placed in five years

q: The carrying (holding) cost of inventory increases with

options.A: a reduction in the number of orders
options.B: faster movement of materials
options.C: shorter lead time from suppliers
options.D: larger average stock held in the depot

q: The ordering cost incurred per order tends to fall when orders are

options.A: placed daily in tiny quantities
options.B: fewer in number and larger in size
options.C: split among many suppliers
options.D: placed only for imported items

q: Administrative lead time in procurement covers the

options.A: transit time of goods by rail or road
options.B: manufacturing time at the supplier's works
options.C: time taken in processing the indent and order within the organisation
options.D: time spent in inspection after receipt

q: Delivery lead time in procurement covers the

options.A: time taken by the supplier from order placement to delivery
options.B: time taken to prepare the annual estimate
options.C: time taken for budget allotment
options.D: time taken to codify a new item

q: Provisioning must account for the total lead time because

options.A: suppliers offer discounts for early orders
options.B: it reduces the number of indents needed
options.C: it eliminates the need for safety stock
options.D: orders must be placed in time for material to be available when needed

q: While analysing consumption trends for provisioning, one should exclude

options.A: the regular monthly consumption figures
options.B: abnormal, non-recurring spikes in consumption
options.C: seasonal variations observed every year
options.D: consumption of the last three years

q: A steadily rising consumption trend for an item indicates that

options.A: the item should be declared obsolete
options.B: provisioning should be reduced below past average
options.C: requirements should be pitched above the past average
options.D: safety stock can be safely reduced to zero

q: The moving average method of demand forecasting

options.A: averages consumption of recent periods to smooth out fluctuations
options.B: gives all weight to the oldest available data
options.C: ignores past consumption completely
options.D: is used only for imported items

q: Exponential smoothing as a forecasting method

options.A: treats all past periods with equal weight
options.B: is applicable only to vital items
options.C: requires no past consumption data
options.D: gives progressively more weight to recent consumption data

q: Seasonal variation in consumption of a store item is handled in forecasting by

options.A: ignoring the months of peak consumption
options.B: adjusting the forecast with seasonal factors
options.C: ordering the full year's need at once
options.D: keeping zero safety stock in lean months

q: Provisioning review is normally conducted by the

options.A: accounts department alone
options.B: supplier's marketing team
options.C: stores department in consultation with user departments
options.D: railway board directly for every item

q: The annual requirements of stores collected from users are consolidated by the

options.A: stores department into a provisioning programme
options.B: personnel department for staff planning
options.C: engineering department for works planning
options.D: commercial department for freight targets

q: User departments submit their annual store requirements to the

options.A: divisional railway manager personally
options.B: general manager's office directly
options.C: chief personnel officer
options.D: stores department

q: Over-provisioning of stores results in

options.A: faster movement of materials
options.B: blockage of capital and risk of obsolescence
options.C: reduction in ordering costs to zero
options.D: improved quality of maintenance work

q: Under-provisioning of stores results in

options.A: lower inventory carrying costs only
options.B: higher discounts from suppliers
options.C: stock-outs causing delays in maintenance and operations
options.D: automatic cancellation of indents

q: Outstanding dues (materials ordered but not received) are considered in provisioning to

options.A: avoid duplicate ordering of the same requirement
options.B: increase the total quantity ordered
options.C: delay payment to the suppliers
options.D: reduce the safety stock to zero

q: Provisioning review checks the realism of demands against

options.A: the seniority of indenting officers
options.B: the colour of storage bins
options.C: prevailing fashion in the market
options.D: past consumption, stock in hand and dues

q: The net quantity to be provisioned is arrived at from

options.A: gross requirement plus total stock in hand
options.B: gross requirement minus stock in hand and dues in, plus dues out
options.C: safety stock multiplied by lead time
options.D: maximum level minus re-order quantity

q: In ABC analysis, 'B' category items comprise

options.A: a moderate number of items with moderate consumption value, needing moderate control
options.B: all imported items irrespective of value
options.C: only obsolete and surplus items
options.D: items that are never reviewed

q: ABC analysis helps the stores department to

options.A: concentrate control efforts on high-value items
options.B: eliminate all low-value items from stock
options.C: fix the same safety stock for every item
options.D: avoid classifying items by criticality

q: VED analysis of stores is based on the

options.A: unit price of each item
options.B: annual consumption value
options.C: alphabetical order of nomenclature
options.D: criticality of the item to operations

q: Compared with a desirable item, a vital spare for a locomotive would normally carry

options.A: zero safety stock
options.B: a higher safety stock
options.C: the same safety stock
options.D: no re-order level at all

q: For a vital item, the re-order level is generally set

options.A: lower than for desirable items
options.B: at zero to save carrying cost
options.C: higher, to ensure no stock-out occurs
options.D: equal to the minimum level

q: The maximum stock level is normally fixed as

options.A: re-order level plus re-order quantity minus minimum consumption during lead time
options.B: twice the safety stock
options.C: half of the annual consumption
options.D: equal to the minimum level

q: The minimum stock level is fixed to cover

options.A: the full year's consumption
options.B: the supplier's manufacturing time only
options.C: annual budget fluctuations
options.D: emergency needs during the replenishment lead time

q: If the lead time of an item is highly variable, provisioning should

options.A: reduce the safety stock
options.B: increase the safety stock
options.C: stop ordering the item
options.D: fix the re-order level at zero

q: Standardisation of stores items helps provisioning by

options.A: increasing the variety of items stocked
options.B: raising the unit price of items
options.C: reducing variety and enabling bulk purchase
options.D: eliminating the need for inspection

q: Codification of stores items assists provisioning because

options.A: each item is uniquely identified, avoiding duplication and confusion
options.B: it increases the price of items
options.C: it removes the need for stock records
options.D: it shortens the shelf life of items

q: Provisioning for imported stores requires

options.A: no lead time allowance
options.B: the same lead time as indigenous items
options.C: provisioning only after receipt
options.D: a longer lead time allowance than indigenous items

q: Annual rate contracts simplify provisioning by

options.A: increasing the tendering time for each order
options.B: fixing prices and sources, thereby shortening procurement lead time
options.C: removing the need for any stock
options.D: making every item a vital item

q: Demand forecasting for a new item with no consumption history uses

options.A: zero requirement for the first year
options.B: the moving average of unrelated items
options.C: judgmental estimates based on similar items
options.D: random quantities decided by lottery

q: The trend projection method of forecasting

options.A: extends the past consumption trend into the future
options.B: ignores all historical data
options.C: is used only for stationery items
options.D: assumes demand will always remain constant

q: The base for calculating the annual requirement of a consumable item is the

options.A: highest consumption in any single month
options.B: budget sanctioned five years ago
options.C: number of suppliers on the approved list
options.D: average annual consumption adjusted for known changes

q: Known future changes considered while provisioning include

options.A: change of the depot in-charge
options.B: addition of new assets and growth in traffic
options.C: colour of the new uniforms
options.D: holidays declared next year

q: During provisioning review, slow-moving and non-moving items are examined for

options.A: immediate bulk re-order
options.B: curtailment of further provisioning and disposal
options.C: reclassification as vital items
options.D: doubling of their safety stock

q: Surplus stores identified during provisioning review are

options.A: offered for transfer to needy units or disposal to release capital
options.B: immediately destroyed without record
options.C: hidden from the stock records
options.D: converted into vital items

q: The provisioning cycle normally starts with the

options.A: receipt of material from suppliers
options.B: payment of suppliers' bills
options.C: disposal of obsolete items
options.D: collection of requirements from user departments

q: In provisioning terminology, 'dues in' means

options.A: demands of users pending with the depot
options.B: quantities already ordered but not yet received
options.C: items declared surplus
options.D: bills pending payment

q: In provisioning terminology, 'dues out' means

options.A: quantities already received from suppliers
options.B: payments overdue to suppliers
options.C: demands of users to be met from stock
options.D: items returned to suppliers

q: The net annual requirement of an item equals

options.A: gross requirement minus stock in hand and dues in
options.B: gross requirement plus safety stock twice
options.C: maximum level plus minimum level
options.D: annual consumption multiplied by lead time

q: Safety stock is also commonly called

options.A: dead stock
options.B: surplus stock
options.C: transit stock
options.D: buffer stock

q: Re-order levels should be

options.A: fixed once for all time
options.B: reviewed periodically as consumption rates and lead times change
options.C: changed daily for every item
options.D: kept secret from user departments

q: A high re-order level relative to consumption rate indicates

options.A: a very short lead time
options.B: zero safety stock
options.C: a long lead time or a high safety stock
options.D: an error in codification

q: Stock-out cost refers to the

options.A: cost of operations delayed or disrupted due to non-availability of material
options.B: price paid to the supplier
options.C: freight charges for urgent despatch
options.D: cost of printing indents

q: The objective of scientific provisioning is to ensure

options.A: maximum variety of items in stock
options.B: zero inventory at all times
options.C: purchase only from a single supplier
options.D: right material in right quantity at right time at minimum cost

q: Provisioning that ignores consumption trends leads to

options.A: perfect matching of stock with needs
options.B: mismatch between stocks held and actual requirements
options.C: automatic standardisation of items
options.D: elimination of safety stock

q: In procurement priority, vital items in VED classification get

options.A: the lowest priority
options.B: priority only after desirable items
options.C: first priority in procurement and stocking
options.D: no priority at all

q: ABC and VED classifications are often combined because

options.A: value and criticality together guide a balanced control policy
options.B: they are identical classifications
options.C: one of them is always wrong
options.D: it doubles the number of items

q: An item that is 'A' in ABC but 'D' in VED needs

options.A: high safety stock and loose value control
options.B: no provisioning at all
options.C: immediate disposal as surplus
options.D: tight value control but low safety stock

q: Provisioning review is done more frequently for

options.A: 'C' and desirable items
options.B: 'A' and vital items
options.C: obsolete items only
options.D: stationery items only

q: A sound provisioning system ultimately aims at

options.A: holding the maximum possible stock
options.B: ordering everything from one supplier
options.C: balancing service level against inventory cost
options.D: eliminating all purchase orders
